title: Heuristic
body:
A function $h(n)$ estimating the cost from node $n$ to a goal. It is a **guess with rules**, and
the rules are what make [[A* Search]] provably correct rather than merely fast.

This is the design work of the whole search block. The algorithm is fixed; choosing $h$ is where
the thinking happens.

## The two properties

**Admissible: $h(n) \le h^*(n)$ for every $n$.** It never overestimates the true remaining cost.
An admissible heuristic is optimistic, and optimism is what keeps $A^*$ honest: the search will
not dismiss a route on the strength of a guess that was too pessimistic.

**Consistent (monotone): $h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n')$ for every edge.** The triangle inequality.
The estimate cannot drop by more than the step actually cost.

Consistency implies admissibility, not the other way round. In practice almost every heuristic
anyone invents is consistent, and the distinction matters for exactly one thing: with a merely
admissible heuristic, $A^*$ may need to re-expand nodes.

| | Admissible | Consistent |
|---|---|---|
| Guarantees | $A^*$ finds an optimal path | that, plus each node expanded once |
| Fails when | it ever overestimates | $f$ ever decreases along a path |
| Example | straight-line distance on a road map | the same one |

## Designing one: relax the problem

**The standard method is to solve an easier version of the problem exactly, and use that answer as
the estimate.** Remove a constraint, and the exact cost in the relaxed problem is a lower bound on
the real cost, so it is admissible by construction.

The 8-puzzle is the worked example everyone uses:

| Relaxation | Heuristic | Typical nodes expanded, depth 24 |
|---|---|---|
| none | brute force | $\sim 10^{10}$ |
| a tile can teleport anywhere | **misplaced tiles**, $h_1$ | ~39000 |
| a tile can move onto any adjacent square, occupied or not | **Manhattan distance**, $h_2$ | ~1600 |

Straight-line distance for road navigation is the same trick: relax "you must follow roads" to
"you may fly", and the crow-flies distance is a lower bound on the driving distance.

## Dominance

If $h_2(n) \ge h_1(n)$ everywhere and both are admissible, **$h_2$ dominates $h_1$** and expands
no more nodes. Bigger is better, right up to the ceiling of $h^*$ itself. So the goal is the
largest admissible estimate you can compute cheaply, and that last clause is the trade: a
heuristic that takes longer to evaluate than the nodes it saves is a loss. Taking
$h = \max(h_1, h_2)$ is always admissible and always dominates both.

## Where else the word turns up

**Careful, it means something looser elsewhere.** In this course a heuristic is a numeric estimate
with provable properties. In general use, and in [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]], it just
means a rule of thumb that usually works. The [[Game Trees]] evaluation function is the middle
case: same job (estimate the value of a position), no guarantee at all, and the horizon effect is
what happens when you trust it.

`Books/Sequential Sorting.md` and [[NP-Complete]] give the reason the whole idea exists: some
problems have no fast exact algorithm, so the options are wait, approximate, or guess well.
